item.title: SoftBank's $7 billion loss lands on the day Anthropic starts selling a $1.1–1.3 trillion IPO
item.description: The largest outside holder of OpenAI just reported its first quarterly loss in two years, and the valuation range for Anthropic's listing has fallen for the third time in a month.
item.content:encoded:
The largest outside holder of OpenAI just reported its first quarterly loss in two years, and the valuation range for Anthropic's listing has fallen for the third time in a month.

SoftBank Group reported a net loss of roughly ¥1.1 trillion, about $7 billion, for the quarter to September 30, the company said on November 10. A year earlier the same quarter produced a ¥2.5 trillion profit, almost all of it an accounting gain on SoftBank's stake in OpenAI after a funding round lifted the private valuation. Three analysts polled by LSEG had expected anything from a ¥233 billion profit to a ¥113 billion loss; the actual figure was far outside that range.

Why SoftBank matters for AI

SoftBank has spent $64.6 billion to assemble a roughly 13% holding in OpenAI, which makes its quarterly accounts the nearest thing public investors have to a mark-to-market on the most valuable private AI company. When OpenAI's valuation rises, SoftBank books gains; when sentiment turns, as it did through a week in which AI stocks sold off after the US midterms and Nvidia's board opened a probe into its chief executive, the same line reverses. Reuters noted that SoftBank's own shares have roughly halved since early June. The group no longer holds Nvidia, having sold that stake in 2025, so its exposure is now almost purely to OpenAI and to the data-centre projects it is financing alongside it.

Anthropic's timing

The loss landed on the morning Anthropic was expected to begin formally marketing its IPO, fifteen days after its public S-1 filing, with investor meetings reportedly scheduled through the week and a Nasdaq debut possible before Thanksgiving. Bloomberg reported that investors now estimate a valuation of $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion. That is the third downward step in a month: $2 trillion was floated in early October, $1.4–1.5 trillion was the talk two weeks ago, and last week's reporting had buyers pushing back on $1.5 trillion.

The revenue line supports a large number by any historical standard. Anthropic's S-1 showed first-half revenue of $16.3 billion, roughly fourteen times the prior-year period, driven by enterprise coding use. But $1.1 trillion is still more than 30 times annualised first-half revenue, and the filing also disclosed around $895 billion of commitments, overwhelmingly for compute and infrastructure. Nvidia agreed last November to invest up to $10 billion, reportedly including a further allocation in the IPO, in exchange for Anthropic running its first gigawatt of capacity on Nvidia hardware.

The counter-argument

SoftBank's quarter is a lagging indicator of a sell-off that has already partly reversed; the Nasdaq recovered on Friday and Monday, and SoftBank's own shares rose sharply on the results day according to market data widgets, which suggests the loss was priced in. Anthropic also cut the price of its top model by 20% on November 9, which bulls read as confidence in volume and margin rather than a scramble for revenue. And the lower valuation range may be exactly what a successful deal needs: a listing priced to rise is better for a company that will return to the market for capital than one priced to the last private mark.

What to watch

The final price range, which should appear once the roadshow has a week of feedback. The lock-up terms and whether existing holders sell. Whether OpenAI, which has filed confidentially, accelerates its own timetable. And SoftBank's next disclosure of the carrying value of its OpenAI stake, which is now the public market's best read on what OpenAI is worth.

item.title: Anthropic's reported $3.4B generator buy makes power a capital expense for AI labs
item.description: Taking over 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar orders is the biggest known power-equipment purchase by an AI company. It tells you how the labs now think about the grid.
item.content:encoded:
Taking over 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar orders is the biggest known power-equipment purchase by an AI company. It tells you how the labs now think about the grid.

The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Anthropic agreed in late September to pay about $3.4 billion for roughly 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators, taking over orders that OnePWR Solutions, a San Antonio power developer, had placed with Caterpillar about two years ago. The FT cited one person with knowledge of the deal; both companies declined to comment. We have not independently confirmed it, and the figures should be read as reported.

The structure matters as much as the size. OnePWR had the orders but needed capital to complete them. Anthropic had planned to buy power from OnePWR as a customer, then instead took over both the equipment orders and the installation work. No company was acquired and no staff moved. In effect, a model developer stepped into the shoes of a power developer because that was faster than waiting for one.

Why 1.7 gigawatts is a big number

A gigawatt is roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. Today's largest AI training campuses are planned in the 1 to 2 gigawatt range, so this single order is on the scale of one flagship site's entire power budget. The FT described it as the largest known single purchase of power equipment by an AI company, a title previously associated with xAI's turbine deployments at its Memphis and Southaven sites, the Memphis installation having drawn a lawsuit over permitting and emissions.

The economic logic is straightforward. In most US markets, connecting a new large load to the grid now takes years. Buying reciprocating gas generators converts an open-ended wait into a delivery schedule, at the cost of owning a fleet of machines and the gas supply, air permits and operations that come with them. For a company whose amended IPO filing lists about $895 billion in commitments, almost all for compute and infrastructure, $3.4 billion to make a slice of that compute usable on time is a rounding error with outsized leverage.

What it signals about the IPO

Anthropic begins marketing its listing this week, and the S-1 has already been read closely for what it admits about energy. A frontier lab buying gas generation outright will be framed two ways. Investors will see a company securing physical capacity rather than relying on partners, which supports the revenue trajectory it is selling. Critics will see a lab that has talked about safety and responsibility choosing fossil generation at scale, days after voters in several states backed measures restricting data-centre development and after OpenAI pledged to cover the full cost of power and grid upgrades for its own sites.

Both readings can be true. The practical point for anyone modelling the sector is that power has moved from an operating cost that utilities deliver to a capital asset that labs buy, own and depreciate. That changes the shape of their balance sheets, the comparables analysts should use, and the political constituency the labs have to manage.

The counter-argument

Owning generation is not obviously the winning strategy. Gas prices are volatile, air permits are increasingly contested, and utilities in several states are moving toward tariffs that make large loads pay for their own grid upgrades, which would narrow the time advantage of self-generation. Hyperscalers with decades of utility relationships may still get to the grid faster than a lab with a fleet of Caterpillars and a two-year-old operations team.

What to watch

Where the generators go. Anthropic has not said, and siting will determine the permitting fight and the local politics. Watch for an updated S-1 amendment that reflects the deal, for Caterpillar's next earnings commentary on data-centre backlog, and for whether OpenAI, Google or Meta follow with equipment purchases of their own rather than power-purchase agreements.

item.title: OpenAI at $1.25T, Anthropic talked down to $1.2–1.3T: the week AI's two giants got repriced
item.description: Both labs are still worth more than almost any company on earth. What changed is that investors started setting the price instead of accepting it.
item.content:encoded:
Both labs are still worth more than almost any company on earth. What changed is that investors started setting the price instead of accepting it.

Two numbers landed within days of each other. On November 6 Reuters reported, and TechCrunch relayed, that OpenAI had closed about $11 billion as the first part of a larger round, at a valuation of roughly $1.25 trillion, with SoftBank and MGX among the participants. The company had reportedly been seeking $1.5 trillion. The same week, reports from Bloomberg and The Information described investors preparing for Anthropic's IPO roadshow, due to start the week of November 9, discussing a valuation around $1.2–1.3 trillion, below figures floated in October, with a smaller raise or a short delay both on the table if AI stocks stay volatile.

What is driving the discount

Three things converged.

Public-market volatility. AI-related stocks had a rough week, and public comparables are what IPO investors price against. A private round closed in a drawdown prices the drawdown in.

Capital intensity in plain view. Anthropic's S-1, filed October 26, put first-half 2026 revenue at roughly $16.3 billion alongside a very large net loss and multi-year compute commitments, including a reported ~$19 billion, 20-year data-centre lease. OpenAI has made comparable infrastructure pledges, including a November 5 commitment to pay the full cost of power and grid upgrades for its sites. Investors can now see the bills, not just the growth.

Adoption data. Ramp's spending index, reported by TechCrunch the same day as the OpenAI round, shows the share of US businesses paying for AI tools flattening after two years of growth. Plateauing adoption is survivable; plateauing adoption during an IPO roadshow is awkward.

What has not changed

Revenue growth at both companies remains extraordinary by any historical standard, and both rounds are still being filled. A $1.25 trillion valuation is a discount to a wish, not a crisis. The IPO itself is the first chance for the public market to price a frontier lab directly, and every private AI valuation on the street will be re-marked against where it trades in the first month.

What to watch

  • The amended S-1 with a price range: that is the moment the roadshow is real.
  • First-month trading in ANT, and whether OpenAI's remaining round closes at the same $1.25 trillion or lower.
  • Enterprise pricing moves from both labs over the next two quarters; pressure on valuation tends to show up as pressure on list prices.
